paras: The attempted lynching of Hayes White took place on April 29, 1881, when a large crowd boarded a train at Forrest City, Arkansas, to lynch White, a Black prisoner accused of killing Sheriff W. F. Beattie of Crittenden County. The conductor had hidden White in the baggage car, and the crowd left without him. White was tried at Marion and hanged there on June 10 before a crowd reported at 2,000, most of them Black.

White, also printed as Hays White, was described by the Memphis Public Ledger as a 'yellow man' of about thirty-two living near Crawfordsville, Crittenden County. The Memphis papers said he was caught at the safe of W. L. Trexler's store and committed for want of $1,500 bail, though White later said he could prove he was elsewhere.

On the road to the jail at Marion, White shot his guard, the Black constable Turner Hendrix (or Hendricks), and disarmed Emmet Swepstone, a young white man riding with them. White said the constable had abused him and fired at him after the first shot. Early on April 21 Sheriff Beattie and Deputy Sheriff Maddox went to White's cabin, where Beattie was shot dead as he entered. White wounded Maddox, took the sheriff's money and weapons, and fled; he later said he fired without knowing who the man was.

The Ledger put the searchers at some 500 men, and the Appeal described mounted squads of Black and white men. White escaped six Forest City men below Augusta on April 26 by swimming the White River, but was then taken near Augusta by ex-sheriff N. W. Mason of Woodruff County.

On April 29 White was carried by train from Little Rock toward Memphis. According to the Memphis Appeal, whose reporter was aboard, a large crowd boarded at Forrest City to lynch him, but conductor McDonald had locked him in the baggage car and told the men he was in the last car. The men searched the train and got off as it started, and White spent the night in the Memphis jail.

On April 30 White was taken by ferryboat to Marion, where a quiet crowd watched him arraigned; the court appointed Colonel Lyle and George Phelan to defend him. A Memphis dispatch said both whites and Blacks had agreed to permit a fair trial, and a Black preacher named Winn, said to have sheltered White, was jailed.

White was convicted on May 3 after the jury deliberated a few minutes, and Judge Cypert sentenced him on May 5 to hang. He was hanged at Marion on June 10 before about 2,000 people, 1,500 of them Black, after a Black minister prayed with him and the crowd joined his hymn.

Only the white press reported the case, naming White's race in nearly every story. Headlines ran from 'A Negro Desperado's Deadly Work' in the Wheeling Intelligencer to the Public Ledger's 'BLOODY FIEND', which called him a 'Burgling Darky'. The Memphis papers supplied the detail, while short dispatches ran in Chicago, Washington, St. Paul, Savannah, Dallas and Bristol.

Lynching was a recurring theme of the coverage. The first wire report said White would be lynched if caught, the Chicago Tribune noted 'Fears of Judge Lynch', and the Appeal recorded bets that he would be lynched at Marion. The Appeal also printed White's own long statement, ending with his wish not to be mobbed.

In June the Chicago Tribune recast White as a 'notorious outlaw' with a past found in none of the Memphis reports, and wrote that the clamor for Judge Lynch had for a time drowned the demand for legal justice.

Whether the Forrest City crowd meant to lynch White was disputed: the Appeal, the Ledger and the Memphis wire said it did, while an unnamed Forrest City citizen wrote to the Appeal that no lynching was contemplated. The Appeal's account came from its own reporter on the train; the denial is a single letter. Reports also differed on whether Hendrix died within minutes, lingered near death, or died later of his wound.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Hayes White
bases: A crowd boarded the train carrying the prisoner at Forrest City with the reported purpose of lynching him and searched it without finding him (A17, A18, A19); he was later legally tried and hanged (A24, A25, A27).

No mob killed White: the Forrest City crowd that reportedly came to lynch him did not find him (A17, A18), a Forrest City citizen denied lynching was intended (A23), and he was executed after a trial and sentence by Judge Cypert (A24, A25, A27).

The Appeal's reporter on the train, the Ledger and the Memphis wire agree that a crowd boarded to lynch White (A17, A18, A19), but a Forrest City citizen's letter to the Appeal denied that lynching was contemplated (A23); the shootings, capture, trial and hanging are corroborated (A3, A5, A10, A12, A24, A27).

accounts.label: White's statement
accounts.gist: White said he was innocent of the burglary, shot Hendricks after the constable abused him and refused him bail or a visit home, and fired on Beattie without knowing who he was after the man snapped a gun at him.

accounts.label: Memphis local accounts
accounts.gist: White shot the constable without warning, finished him as he lay wounded, ambushed Beattie and robbed his body.

framing.detail: The Public Ledger headed its account 'BLOODY FIEND' and called White a 'Burgling Darky' and 'diabolical a villain'; it reported the Forrest City attempt without comment.
Wire copy in Wheeling, Chicago and Washington called White a 'negro desperado' and stated flatly that he 'will be lynched if caught'.
The Memphis Appeal reported the lynching attempt and betting on a lynching, then printed a denial and stressed that the law would take its course.
The Chicago Tribune's June story described the earlier 'clamor for Judge Lynch' and presented the legal hanging as justice satisfied.
